extracted.intended_audience: funding panelists, program officers, and academic applicants involved in grant/fellowship review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for assessing interdisciplinary research proposals and how diversity considerations are factored into funding decisions. Covers features of 'good' interdisciplinarity, pitfalls, evidence and disciplinary endorsement, plus multiple forms of diversity used as selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity: four manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinarity typically involves (1) developing conceptual links by using a perspective in one discipline to modify a perspective in another discipline, (2) using research techniques developed in one discipline to elaborate a theoretical model in another, (3) developing a new theoretical framework that reconceptualizes research in two or more domains as it attempts to integrate them, and (4) modifying a theoretical framework characteristic of one domain and then applying it to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinct manifestations to identify what kind of interdisciplinarity a proposal pursues; each has different evaluation needs and potential pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good interdisciplinarity = breadth, parsimony, and soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: The best interdisciplinary proposals successfully combine breadth, parsimony, and soundness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for applicants who 'master several fields,' can 'talk the talk' of multiple disciplines, recognize cutting edges, take well-judged gambles, and have training and collaborators that indicate capacity to carry out ambitious integrative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogic character / speaks across disciplinary idioms
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal must 'speak to different disciplines simultaneously' — able to reach people outside the applicant's field and 'speak across disciplinary idioms to a majority of people on the panel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proposal is framed so specialists from multiple disciplines can understand its relevance and contribute to judging its merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary projects should be integrative — bringing together ideas and approaches from different disciplines rather than merely juxtaposing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether integration meaningfully combines approaches/theory rather than being a collection of disconnected methods or citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreach / over-ambitiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Overreaching or excessive ambition is a primary concern: projects that try to reach too far beyond the author's capacity may be 'attractive and fatal' — risky because the person might not be able to do what they propose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of proposals whose scope exceeds plausible execution given the applicant’s background, team, and plan; identify and penalize unrealistic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficiality and shoddy cross-disciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary scholars bear the burden of not doing 'shoddy work' in disciplines they borrow from; superficial grounding in other fields is a common failing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that disciplinary knowledge from borrowed fields is accurate, contextually grounded, and not merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical or 'flashy' interdisciplinarity ('fast and loose')
rubrics_metrics.description: Flashiness or using other disciplines as a rhetorical strategy (e.g., 'throwing in' theorists or concepts without deep application) is a danger: 'fast and loose' projects tag phrases and do not apply theories deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuinely applied interdisciplinary method/theory from projects that merely cite fashionable names or concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplines' toolkits used in a disciplined way
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective interdisciplinarity means using 'other fields' toolkits' consciously and in disciplined ways rather than inventing idiosyncratic standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proposal brokers useful relations between toolkits and follows recognizable disciplinary procedures where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with previous research
rubrics_metrics.description: One criterion for assessing interdisciplinarity is consistency with previous research in the relevant fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the proposal accurately situates itself within and builds on existing literatures across relevant disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between interdisciplinary perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether perspectives from the different disciplines involved are balanced rather than dominated by a single disciplinary viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence that the project treats each disciplinary contribution substantively and not merely nominally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the interdisciplinary approach is likely to be effective in producing the claimed results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider feasibility of methods, coherence of integration, and track record or pilot evidence indicating the approach can work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsement by disciplinary specialists (first-tier certification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful sequence is: secure endorsement from specialists who feel the work 'will satisfy needs in your particular discipline' before applying broader interdisciplinary criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require or value evidence that disciplinary experts would judge the work competent in the relevant local expertises (e.g., publication record, letters, disciplinary benchmarks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance beyond the local discipline (second-tier criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: After disciplinary competence, ask: 'Is it going to do anything for the rest of us?' — i.e., does the work have broader significance across fields?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the potential for the project to contribute to other disciplines, policy, or public knowledge beyond its core field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence: plausible, persuasive, and appropriate evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In interdisciplinary evaluation, traditional questions become: 'Is the argument plausible, persuasive, how is evidence used?' but it can be hard for panelists to judge whether the most appropriate evidence is being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, consult specialists for domain-specific evidence judgments; otherwise evaluate general evidentiary logic, clarity, and transparency of data/method selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting both expert (virtuosity) and generalist (significance) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary proposals often face 'double jeopardy' — they must meet both expert standards (virtuosity) and broader significance standards at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require applicants to demonstrate mastery in relevant local expertise and also articulate transferable contributions; penalize proposals that lack in either dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallback to disciplinary standards when interdisciplinarity ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, evaluators often fall back on existing disciplinary standards when interdisciplinary standards are underdeveloped or ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit in panels about when disciplinary criteria are being applied to interdisciplinary work, and document rationale to ensure fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergent/hybrid nature of interdisciplinary evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for interdisciplinary evaluation are hybrids — emergent and developed through practice and deliberation — which can broaden and multiply criteria and complicate consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that criteria may evolve during deliberations; strive to articulate shared standards early to reduce arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and representativeness as evaluative consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels factor in members' interdisciplinary orientation; panelists should be somewhat representative of the broader population, and panel composition affects what gets funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers should assemble panels with the expertise mix needed to judge proposals; panels should avoid homogeneity (e.g., winners all from a few institutions) that undermines legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-discrimination and explicit diversity policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Some funders explicitly require that panelists 'do not discriminate' and explicitly invite applications from women and minorities; panels are generally asked not to discriminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uphold non-discrimination policies and, where applicable, follow funder guidance encouraging underrepresented applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of diversity used as selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists consider multiple forms of diversity as criteria: institutional diversity, disciplinary diversity, topics diversity, gender, ethno-racial, and geographic diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different competitions and panels weight these types differently; be explicit about which forms the panel values in its mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity as additive / tie-breaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity often acts as an additive criterion rather than an alternative to excellence — frequently used as a tie-breaker among 'maybe' proposals when consensus on excellence is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diversity to decide among comparably rated proposals, not to replace demonstrated quality; document how diversity considerations influenced decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity valued as intrinsic good and means to redress inequities
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity is valued both as an intrinsic good (richer academic environment) and as a means of redressing past injustices, leveling the playing field, and shaping the academic pipeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for diversity-based selections, articulate whether the rationale is intrinsic value, equity/compensation, pipeline-building, or some combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualizing applicant constraints when judging 'polishedness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists are aware that applicants from heavy teaching loads or less-resourced institutions may submit less 'polished' proposals; this context can justify factoring in diversity considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider resource and context signals (institutional teaching loads, access to networks) in evaluating proposal polish, and avoid equating polish solely with scholarly merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promoting diversity to shape the future professoriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists sometimes consider the long-term effect of awards on the composition of the academy, seeing fellowships as a gateway that can increase representation of diverse backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pipeline effects as a legitimate evaluative consideration when aligned with the funder's mission; be transparent about such intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive reliance on a single criterion (excellence vs diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Healthy deliberation involves 'competing criteria put forward vigorously' and tempering one's criteria with consideration of alternative criteria; trouble arises when one criterion is used to exclusion of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage panels to actively debate and balance excellence and diversity, and to make trade-offs explicit rather than hidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel deliberation dynamics affect criteria application
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists apply different standards as deliberations progress: top consensus awards are decided primarily on academic excellence, while other factors (relevance, field diversity, institutional range) gain weight later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that threshold effects occur during deliberation; document the stages and rationale when standards shift between early consensus choices and later tie-breaking discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for possible conservative bias among older panelists
rubrics_metrics.description: Some panels (and older scholars) may be more conservative and 'unwilling... to approach judging' interdisciplinary work, affecting fair evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate bias through panel training, inclusion of interdisciplinary-minded members, and explicit criteria to lower the risk that conservatism blocks fair assessment.
